title: Pearl
description: Hard object produced within a living shelled mollusc
wiki_lead:
A pearl is a hard, shiny object produced within the soft tissue (specifically the mantle) of a living shelled mollusk. Like the shell of a mollusk, a pearl is composed of calcium carbonate (mainly aragonite or a mixture of aragonite and calcite) in a crystalline form, which is deposited in concentric layers. More commercially valuable pearls are perfectly round and smooth, but many other shapes, known as baroque pearls, can occur. The highest quality of natural pearls have been highly valued as gemstones and objects of beauty for many centuries. In literature, pearls have become a metaphor for something rare, fine, admirable, and valuable.
The most valuable pearls occur spontaneously in the wild but are extremely rare. These wild pearls are referred to as natural pearls. Cultured or farmed pearls from pearl oysters and freshwater mussels make up the majority of those currently sold. Imitation pearls are also widely sold in inexpensive jewelry. Pearls have been harvested and cultivated primarily for use in jewelry but in the past were also used to adorn clothing. They have also been crushed and used in cosmetics, medicines, and paint formulations.
Whether wild or cultured, gem-quality pearls are almost always nacreous and iridescent, like the interior of the shell that produces them. However, almost all species of shelled mollusks are capable of producing pearls (technically "calcareous concretions") of lesser shine or less spherical shape. Although these may also be legitimately referred to as "pearls" by gemological labs and also under U.S. Federal Trade Commission rules, and are formed in the same way, most of them have no value except as curiosities.

Etymology
The English word pearl comes from the French perle, originally from the Latin perna 'leg', after the ham- or mutton-leg-shaped bivalve.
The scientific name for the family of pearl-bearing oysters, Margaritiferidae comes from the Old Persian word for pearl *margārīta- which is the source of the English name Margaret.


Definition

All shelled mollusks can, by natural processes, produce some kind of "pearl" when an irritating microscopic object becomes trapped within its mantle folds, but the great majority of these "pearls" are not valued as gemstones. Nacreous pearls, the best-known and most commercially significant, are primarily produced by two groups of molluskan bivalves or clams. A nacreous pearl is made from layers of nacre, by the same living process as is used in the secretion of the mother of pearl, which lines the shell.
Natural (or wild) pearls, formed without human intervention, are very rare. Many hundreds of pearl oysters or mussels must be gathered and opened, and thus killed, to find even one wild pearl. For many centuries, this was the only way pearls were obtained, and why pearls fetched such extraordinary prices in the past. Cultured pearls are formed in pearl farms, using human intervention as well as natural processes.
Saltwater pearls can grow in several species of marine pearl oysters in the family Pteriidae including the pearl oyster. Freshwater pearls grow within certain species of freshwater mussels in the order Unionida, the families Unionidae and Margaritiferidae. These are the river mussels such as the freshwater pearl mussel.


Physical properties

The unique luster of pearls depends upon the reflection, refraction, and diffraction of light from the translucent layers. The thinner and more numerous the layers in the pearl, the finer the luster. The iridescence that pearls display is caused by the overlapping of successive layers, which breaks up light falling on the surface. In addition, pearls (especially cultured freshwater pearls) can be dyed yellow, green, blue, brown, pink, purple, or black. The most valuable pearls have a metallic, highly reflective luster.

grok_lead: A pearl is an organic gem formed within the soft tissue of a living shelled mollusk, such as an oyster or mussel, as layers of nacre âa crystalline form of calcium carbonate known as aragonite âare secreted around an irritant to protect the mollusk. These gems occur naturally or through culturing, where humans implant a nucleus to stimulate nacre production, and they are prized for their lustrous, iridescent appearance, which results from the overlapping platelets of aragonite reflecting light. Unlike most gems, pearls are not mined from the earth but harvested from marine or freshwater environments, making them unique among birthstones as the traditional June birthstone alongside alexandrite and moonstone. Pearls have been treasured for millennia, with the earliest written reference dating to 2206 BC in Chinese records, and they served as symbols of wealth, purity, and status across ancient civilizations in Asia, Europe, and the Americas. Prior to European exploration, primary sources included the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, rivers in China and Europe, and coastal regions of Ceylon (modern Sri Lanka); Christopher Columbus encountered significant oyster beds during his 1498 and 1502 voyages to Venezuela and Panama, though overharvesting led to their decline within a century. In cultural lore, pearls were linked to the moon's spherical form and believed to embody the life-giving essence of water, while in ancient China, they were thought to offer protection from fire and mythical dragons; European traditions associated them with modesty, chastity, and marital harmony. In modern culture, pearls continue to symbolize purity, wisdom, and enduring love, and a classic pearl necklace or pearl stud earrings are widely regarded as a timeless luxury gift from a daughter to her mother to express appreciation, offering sophisticated elegance that remains in style. The four major types of cultured pearls dominate the modern market: Akoya pearls, primarily from saltwater oysters in Japan and China, are typically small (3â10 mm), round, and white or cream-colored with high luster, making them ideal for classic jewelry. South Sea pearls, harvested from large oysters in Australia, Indonesia, and the Philippines, are among the largest (9â20 mm), often round or near-round, and feature white, silver, or golden hues with thick nacre layers that enhance their value. Tahitian pearls, from French Polynesia's black-lip oysters, range from 8â16 mm in size and display dark colors like gray, black, or brown with colorful overtones (e.g., green, purple), earning them the nickname "black pearls" despite their iridescent variety. Freshwater pearls, produced in mussels mainly from China, offer the widest range of shapes and sizes (2â13 mm), come in diverse colors including white, pink, and lavender, and are more affordable due to higher yields per mollusk (up to 50 pearls). Natural pearls, free of human intervention, are exceedingly rare today and command premium prices based on factors like size, shape, luster, surface quality, and nacre thickness.
